Mineral grains and organic matter, as one solid of nominal molar mass; what lives and dissolves in it is in its water (a wet solid). A loam's field capacity (0.4 mL/g); its extractable mineral nitrogen is low (about 5 mg N/kg, as ammonium) and its phosphate moderate (about 23 mg P/kg), so bacteria growing on a hydrocarbon in it run short of nitrogen first.
A solvent for compounds that do not dissolve in water; bacteria tolerate a few per cent, so a solvent-only control shows it has no effect at the concentration used.
As a carbon source in a minimal medium: organisms that can use it (marker glucose+) grow on it with mineral nitrogen and phosphorus, about 4 g/L supporting full density (illustrative).
Carbonic acid's pKa values 6.35 and 10.33 (ideal solution): with sodium bicarbonate it buffers near pH 10.
See sodium carbonate.

A fast, high-capacity drying agent for organic solutions: it takes up to seven waters each as the heptahydrate (about 1 g of water per gram). Fine powder that clumps as it hydrates; while some stays free-flowing when swirled, the solution is dry.
What anhydrous magnesium sulfate becomes as it dries a solution: clumped, and holding whatever the water it took up had dissolved.
Followed only in liquids that declare it: air-saturated water holds about 8.9 mg/L at 21 °C (models/gases.ts).
A ketose: it reduces Benedict’s reagent because alkali turns it into an enediol (and so into aldoses).

A triglyceride oil as triolein: insoluble in water, it floats as its own layer; fat-soluble dyes (Sudan III) go into it.

An inert electrode: it neither dissolves nor reacts. A 6 mm rod (4/(ρd) = 0.0003 m²/g). Hydrogen and oxygen form on it only some 0.6 and 1.0 V beyond their equilibrium potentials at classroom currents, which is why chlorine, not oxygen, comes off concentrated brine.
